readerTitle: Ford was losing billions, and every chart said green
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Ford, 2006~2009년 Alan Mulally의 회생) + 가상 적용 (소프트웨어 회사)
insight: 위기에서 리더가 실제로 보는 현실은 첫 나쁜 소식을 가져온 사람에게 보인 반응만큼만 정확하다.
misconception: 위기에는 통제를 조이고 책임자를 찾아 문책하는 강한 리더가 필요하다.

sources.text: Hoffman, B. (2012). American Icon: Alan Mulally and the Fight to Save Ford Motor Company. Crown Business. (Business Plan Review 회의, 색깔 차트, Mark Fields의 Edge 빨간불 일화)
Ford Motor Company, 2006 Annual Report / Form 10-K (2006년 순손실)
Ford Motor Company, 2009 Annual Report / Form 10-K (2009년 흑자 전환)
Ford press releases: 2006년 말 자산 담보 대출, 2012년 담보 해제와 블루 오벌 로고 회수
Ford press releases on brand sales: Aston Martin (2007), Jaguar Land Rover to Tata Motors (2008), Volvo to Geely (2010)

factChecks.note: Mulally는 2006년 9월 Boeing 상용기 부문에서 Ford CEO로 옮겼습니다. 날짜를 다시 확인하세요.
2006년 Ford 순손실은 약 127억 달러로 널리 보도되었습니다. 카드에는 수치 없이 "a record loss"로만 적었습니다. 10-K로 확인하세요.
Edge 출시 문제(캐나다 Oakville 공장, 리프트게이트 부품 문제)와 Mulally가 박수를 쳤다는 장면은 Hoffman(2012)에 근거한 일화입니다. 정확한 발언은 인용하지 않고 "reportedly"로 표시했습니다. 회의실 사람들이 Fields의 해고를 예상했다는 부분도 같은 책 기준입니다.
2006년 말 자산 대부분과 블루 오벌 로고를 담보로 약 236억 달러를 조달한 사실은 널리 보도되었습니다. 카드에는 금액을 적지 않았습니다.
Ford는 2009년 GM·Chrysler와 달리 파산 절차와 긴급 구제금융을 피했습니다. 다만 미국 에너지부의 첨단기술차량 대출 프로그램 자금은 받았으므로 카드에 "emergency bailout"으로 한정해 적었습니다. 2009년 흑자 전환도 연차보고서로 확인하세요.
BPR 회의 규칙(매주, 모든 임원 참석, 같은 형식, 녹·황·적 색깔 표시)은 Hoffman(2012)과 다수 언론 인터뷰에 나옵니다. 세부 규칙 문구는 요약해서 적었습니다.

cards.title: Ford was losing billions, and every chart said green
body: In 2006, Ford was heading for a record loss. It had just hired a new CEO from Boeing, Alan Mulally.
Each week, his top executives showed their status charts, coded green, yellow or red. Week after week, almost every chart was green.

image.label: Boardroom wall of status charts, all green
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 어두운 회의실 벽에 상태 차트 여러 장이 모두 초록색으로 빛나고, 창밖으로 텅 빈 자동차 주차장과 아래로 꺾인 그래프가 보임. 실제 자동차 브랜드 로고나 엠블럼은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Finally, someone shows a red.
body: You're the new CEO. The company is losing money fast, yet your leaders report almost nothing wrong.
Then the head of your largest region marks a new car launch red. A part problem is holding it up at a plant. The room goes quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Ask who is responsible and set a hard deadline for a fix
options.feedback: It feels decisive and shows you take problems seriously. But everyone watching learns that red gets you questioned, so next week the charts turn green again.

options.text: Thank him in front of everyone and ask who can help
options.feedback: You give up a show of toughness. In return, the room learns that honest reporting is safe, and the problem gets more hands.

options.text: Move on quickly and discuss it with him privately later
options.feedback: It spares him embarrassment, but the room never sees how you treat bad news. Silence can read as disapproval.

cards.title: He clapped.
body: The executive was Mark Fields, who ran Ford's Americas business. The problem was delaying the launch of the Ford Edge. According to journalist Bryce Hoffman's account, some in the room expected Fields to be fired.
Instead, Mulally reportedly applauded, called it great visibility, and asked who could help. Other executives offered ideas, and the issue was worked on quickly.
The next week, the charts came in full of yellow and red. For the first time, the meeting showed the real company.

cards.title: Your first reaction sets the reporting system
body: In a crisis, a leader's first job is to **see reality fast**. But leaders rarely see problems themselves. They see what people choose to tell them.
People decide what to tell you by watching how you treat the first person who brings bad news. One public reaction teaches the whole room more than any memo about openness.
Mulally didn't need better charts. He needed people willing to color them honestly.

image.label: One red chart turning a wall of green into a mix of colors
image.brief: 두 장면 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 모두 초록색인 차트 벽, 한 장만 빨간색이고 그 앞에서 박수 치는 손. 오른쪽: 다음 주, 초록·노랑·빨강이 섞인 차트 벽. 가운데 화살표 "One reaction". 실제 인물 얼굴이나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A meeting built to make problems visible
body: Mulally's weekly Business Plan Review ran on simple, firm habits:
list: **Every week, same time:** no skipping, no sending a deputy
**Same format for everyone:** the same charts and color codes
**Red means help needed:** the room works on it together
**Focus on the plan, not the person:** no blame, no side jokes
cards.callout: Red stopped meaning "you failed" and started meaning "we know where to act."

cards.title: The usual crisis playbook would have backfired.
body: The common instinct in a crisis is to tighten control and find who's to blame. It looks strong. But it teaches people to hide problems until they explode, so the leader steers with a false map.
Ford went the other way. In 2009, when GM and Chrysler went through bankruptcy with emergency government bailouts, Ford avoided both. It returned to profit that same year.

cards.title: Honest charts didn't save Ford alone.
body: Ford had borrowed heavily in late 2006, pledging most of its assets, even its blue oval logo, before credit markets froze. It sold Jaguar, Land Rover, Aston Martin and later Volvo, and made deep cuts.

Praising red also works only if two things follow. Problems must actually get fixed. And a red that never turns yellow still needs someone accountable for it. Safety to report is not freedom from results.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You run a 40-person software company. Your biggest customer has been promised a feature by the end of the month. The weekly status board has been green for weeks.
In the team meeting, a junior engineer says the feature will slip by three weeks. Her manager looks annoyed. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her for flagging it early, then ask the team what would help most
options.feedback: You lose nothing but a comfortable illusion. You gain three weeks to reset the customer's expectations or add help, and a team that keeps telling you the truth.

options.text: Ask why this wasn't raised sooner
options.feedback: It's a fair question, but asked now, in public, it punishes the one person who spoke up. Ask it later, about the process, not her.

options.text: Tell the team to find a way to hit the date
options.feedback: It shows commitment to the customer. But it may push the team to cut quality or hide the next delay instead of solving it.

cards.title: Reward the first red, and you'll see the rest.
body: In a crisis, how you react to bad news decides whether you hear the next piece in time to act.
**Try it today:** the next time someone brings you a problem, say thank you before you ask any question.
